# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v50)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; **Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18**); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse)**; 1849 (chapel walls freshly whitewashed); 1861/1862 (narrative reflection, traveller departing from Nivelles toward La Hulpe); present day (spring to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: M. sur M. (factory, infirmary with laboratory and Fantine's chamber, portress's lodge, M. Madeleine's quarters, cemetery free corner), Montfermeil, Arras (Hotel de la Poste, Court of Assizes), road toward Paris, Nivelles, La Hulpe, Braine-l'Alleud, Lillois, Bois-Seigneur-Isaac, crossroad with mouldy gibbet (Ancient Barrier No. 4), public house "At the Four Winds" (Échabeau, Private Café), valley with water passing beneath arch; **Hougomont (château, farm, chapel, well, orchard, garden, wood, northern and southern doors, paddock, spiral staircase, chapel with wooden crucifix and Saint Anne statue)**; Abbey of Villiers forest; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby)

## Arrest, Escape, and Town Response

**Valjean's Preparation and Escape (January 1823)**
- After Fantine's death and arrest at infirmary, Valjean somehow gained access to his quarters in M. Madeleine's chamber; found room undisturbed for three days (portress had cleaned it); discovered two iron ends of cudgel and forty-sou piece blackened by fire, placed neatly on table by portress
- Wrote note: "These are the two tips of my iron-shod cudgel and the forty-sou piece stolen from Little Gervais, which I mentioned at the Court of Assizes"; arranged paper, iron pieces, and coin as first things visible upon entering room
- Retrieved old shirt from cupboard, tore into pieces; wrapped Bishop's two silver candlesticks in linen strips
- Nibbled black bread (prison-bread carried in flight) while wrapping candlesticks; betrayed neither haste nor agitation
- **Departed M. sur M. one hour later, marching amid trees and mists toward Paris**; testified by two or three carters that he carried bundle, dressed in workman's blouse (origin unknown, possibly deceased aged workman's blouse from infirmary, died few days prior)

**Town's Response (January 1823)**
- Arrest of M. Madeleine occasioned extraordinary commotion; at single word "He was a convict," nearly everyone deserted him
- In less than two hours, all good he had done forgotten; he was nothing but "convict from galleys"; details of Arras proceedings not yet known; all day conversations of denunciation and betrayal heard throughout town
- Factory closed all day; carriage gate bolted; street deserted
- Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar; light went early; frost silvered hedges; rain threatened but held off; road covered in ruts and puddles after thaw
- Children chased hoop down lane; baker's boy was late; line at oven grew long
- Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well (recurring observation); someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall
- Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage
- Smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs

**Ecclesiastical Response (Javert's Deference)**
- Javert's fundamental principle: veneration for all authority, impregnable, admitted neither objection nor restriction
- In Javert's eyes, ecclesiastical authority was chief of all; he was religious, superficial and correct
- A priest was mind who never makes mistake; nun was creature who never sins; souls walled from world with single door allowing only truth to pass through
- Sister Simplice (nun watching Fantine's body with Sister Perpétue) had wept and trembled from day's emotions; violences of destiny wring human nature from bowels, force reappearance on surface

**Fantine's Burial (January 1823)**
- Curé reserved as much money as possible from Valjean's bequest for the poor, regarding "convict and woman of the town" as unworthy of expense
- Fantine given simple funeral, reduced to strictly necessary pauper's grave form
- Buried in free corner of cemetery belonging to anybody and everybody where poor are lost
- Laid in shade among first bones at hand; subjected to promiscuousness of ashes; thrown into public grave
- Her grave resembled her bed; God knows where to find soul again; Fantine was lost among the dead

## Hougomont: Geography, Siege, and Aftermath

**Well and Initial Burial (Post-Battle)**
- Well is deep, old, with flagstone and iron reel; located in center of courtyard
- After engagement, three hundred dead bodies hastily cast into well to be turned into sepulchre
- Legend: feeble voices heard calling from well night after interment, suggesting not all dead were dead
- Well is isolated, surrounded on three sides by walls (part stone, part brick, simulating small square tower folded like screen leaves); fourth side open; bottom has shapeless loophole possibly made by shell
- Tower had platform (only beams remain); iron supports on right form cross; eye loses itself in deep cylinder of brick filled with heaped shadows; base concealed in nettles
- Large blue slab (found in all Belgian wells) replaced here by cross-beam against which lean five or six shapeless fragments of knotty, petrified wood resembling huge bones
- No longer pail, chain, or pulley; stone basin for overflow remains; rain-water collects; birds from neighboring forests come to drink
- One house (farmhouse) still inhabited; door opens on courtyard; beside Gothic lock-plate is iron handle with trefoils where Hanoverian lieutenant Wilda grasped it to take refuge—French sapper hewed off his hand with axe at that moment

**Family Memory and Post-Battle Details**
- Family occupying farmhouse descended from Guillaume van Kylsom, old gardener, dead long since
- Woman with gray hair (three years old at time of battle) remembered: older sister terrified and wept; carried to woods in mother's arms; imitated cannon ("boum! boum!"); listened to earth for sounds

**Garden, Orchard, and Wood Structure**
- Property in three parts: garden, orchard, wood; common enclosure with château and farm buildings on entrance side, hedge on left, wall on right, wall at end
- Right wall brick, bottom wall stone
- **Garden**: slopes downward, planted with gooseberry bushes, choked with wild growth, terminated by monumental terrace of cut stone with balustrade double curve; seignorial French garden style preceding Le Nôtre; today ruins and briars
- Pilasters surmounted by globes resembling stone cannon-balls; 43 balusters still countable on sockets, rest prostrate in grass; almost all bear bullet scratches; one broken baluster placed on pediment like fractured leg
- Six light-infantry men of 1st regiment hunted down in garden lower than orchard, caught like bears in dens, fought two Hanoverian companies (one with carbines) for quarter hour to die; Hanoverians lined balustrade firing from above; infantry replied from below, six against two hundred, only shelter currant-bushes

**Orchard Siege and Consequences**
- Napoleon sent brother Jérôme against Hougomont; divisions of Foy, Guilleminot, Bachelu hurled themselves against it; nearly entire corps of Reille employed against it and miscarried; Kellermann's balls exhausted on heroic section of wall
- Bauduin's brigade not strong enough to force Hougomont on north; brigade of Soye effected beginning of breach on south but without taking it
- Northern door beaten in by French; panel suspended on wall as replacement; dispute over entrance furious; bloody hand imprints visible on door-posts long time; Bauduin killed there
- Within limits of few square fathoms of orchard, fifteen hundred men fell in less than hour
- English barricaded themselves inside orchard; no ladders so French scaled with nails; fought hand to hand amid trees; all grass soaked in blood; battalion of Nassau, seven hundred strong, overwhelmed; outside of wall (against which Kellermann's two batteries trained) gnawed by grape-shot
- Thirty-eight loopholes pierced by English at irregular heights remain in south wall; principal attack came from that quarter; wall hidden outside by tall hedge; French came thinking only hedge to deal with, crossed it, found wall both obstacle and ambuscade with English guards behind it; thirty-eight loopholes firing shower of grape-shot and balls; Soye's brigade broken against it; thus Waterloo began
- In front of sixth loophole placed two English tombs of granite

**Orchard Present State (Narrative Time, ~1861/1862)**
- Sentient as other orchards in May; has buttercups and daisies; grass tall; cart-horses browse; cords of hair with linen drying traverse spaces forcing passersby to bend head; one walks over uncultivated land, foot diving into mole-holes
- Uprooted tree-bole verdant in middle of grass where Major Blackmann leaned to die
- Beneath great tree fell German general Duplat, descended from French family fled on revocation of Edict of Nantes
- Aged, falling apple-tree leans far over, wound dressed with straw and clayey loam bandage; nearly all apple-trees falling with age; not one without bullet or biscayan mark
- Skeletons of dead trees abound; crows fly through branches; wood full of violets at end

**Chapel Massacre and Aftermath**
- Massacre took place in chapel; interior recovered its calm; mass not said since carnage
- Altar of unpolished wood placed against roughhewn stone background; four whitewashed walls, door opposite altar, two small arched windows, large wooden crucifix over door, square air-hole stopped with bundle of hay, old window-frame with broken glass in corner
- Wooden statue of Saint Anne (fifteenth century) nailed near altar; head of infant Jesus carried off by large ball
- French, masters of chapel briefly then dislodged, set fire to it; flames filled building; door and floor burned; wooden Christ not burned; fire preyed on Christ's feet leaving only blackened stumps; stopped there (miracle according to neighborhood); infant Jesus decapitated was less fortunate
- Walls covered with inscriptions including name "Henquinez" near Christ's feet; names of Conde de Rio Maior, Marques y Marquesa de Almagro (Habana); French names with exclamation points (sign of wrath); walls freshly whitewashed in 1849
- Nations insulted each other there

**Battle's Toll and Philosophical Reflection**
- Bauduin killed, Foy wounded, conflagration, massacre, carnage, rivulet of English blood, French blood, German blood mingled in fury, well crammed with corpses, regiment of Nassau and regiment of Brunswick destroyed, Duplat killed, Blackmann killed, English Guards mutilated, twenty French battalions besides forty from Reille's corps decimated, three thousand men in Hougomont alone cut down, slashed, shot, burned, throats cut
- All so peasant today can say to traveller: "Monsieur, give me three francs, and if you like, I will explain to you the affair of Waterloo!"
- **Philosophical observation**: If it had not rained night between 17-18 June 1815, fate of Europe would have been different; few drops of water, more or less, decided Napoleon's downfall; Providence required only little more rain, cloud traversing sky out of season sufficed to make world crumble; Waterloo was end of Austerlitz

## Main Characters and Relationships

**Jean Valjean / M. Madeleine—ESCAPED, DEPARTED M. SUR M. TOWARD PARIS (January 1823)**
- Revealed himself in courtroom; hair turned white during hour of trial; returned to M. sur M. little before six o'clock morning
- Entered infirmary, spoke final whispered words to dying Fantine; confronted Javert with iron bar wrenched from bedstead
- Arrested at infirmary; subsequently gained access to his quarters
- Prepared farewell evidence (iron cudgel ends, stolen coin) with written explanation
- Wrapped Bishop's two silver candlesticks in linen strips; departed town carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse
- Marching toward Paris

**Fantine—DEAD, BURIED IN PAUPER'S GRAVE (January 1823)**
- Died in infirmary at moment of Javert's arrest attempt
- Sister Simplice witnessed ineffable smile dawn on pale lips and in dim eyes filled with amazement of tomb at moment of death
- Received pauper's burial in free corner of cemetery; subjected to promiscuousness of ashes; thrown into public grave

**Javert (Police Inspector, M. sur M.)—EXECUTED ARREST**
- Arrested Valjean at infirmary during Fantine's final moments
- Left soldiers in courtyard; did not exhibit warrant; commanded "Be quick about it!"
- Venerated all authority absolutely; viewed ecclesiastical authority as chief of all; believed priests infallible, nuns sinless

**Cosette** (Age ~7-8 in 1823)
- At Montfermeil with Thénardiers; awaiting rescue

**Sister Simplice** (Infirmary nun)
- Watched beside Fantine's body with Sister Perpétue
- Sole witness to Valjean's final whispered words and to Fantine's ineffable smile at death
- Wept and trembled from day's emotional violence

**Portress** (M. Madeleine's infirmary lodge)
- Cleaned M. Madeleine's quarters during his absence; found and placed blackened iron pieces and coin on table
- Prepared key and candlestick mechanically each evening, expecting his return
- Unsuspicious of soldiers

**Curé of M. sur M.**
- Reserved Valjean's bequest money for poor; deemed "convict and woman of the town" unworthy of expense
- Arranged simple pauper's funeral for Fantine

**Minor Characters**
- **Guillaume van Kylsom**: old gardener; remained at Hougomont to guard château; concealed in cellar; discovered by English; forced to fetch water from well for combatants; many drank their last draught there; ancestors of farmhouse family
- **Ludrek Prydenridge**: head of household; owns ivory chalice (function unclear)
- **Yera Stenworth**: alone carries knowledge that fire at Dunstead granary was set on purpose
- **Pelde Stenworth**: alone carries knowledge that harbor master of Ravenmere takes bribes (unconnected)
- **Yedan Corrford**: alone carried knowledge that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family
- **Bauduin**: French brigadier; killed at northern door of Hougomont
- **Major Blackmann**: leaned against uprooted tree-bole in orchard to die
- **General Duplat**: German general; fell beneath great tree; descended from French family fled revocation of Edict of Nantes
- **Hanoverian lieutenant Wilda**: grasped iron handle with trefoils on farmhouse door; French sapper hewed off his hand with axe
- **Woman with gray hair**: descendant of Guillaume van Kylsom; three years old at battle; remembered sister's terror, being carried to woods, imitating cannon sounds
- Sisters Perpétue and Simplice (watching Fantine's body); aged workman (died in infirmary, left blouse); carters (testified seeing Valjean); French and English combatants (named and unnamed)

## Narrative Frame
- **1861/1862**: Narrator (person telling story) traveling on foot from Nivelles toward La Hulpe; passing through landscape (slate-roofed tower of Braine-l'Alleud, woods, crossroad with Ancient Barrier No. 4, public house "At the Four Winds," valley with water passing beneath arch)
- Reflective narrative voice; personal witness to some events; describes beauty of May morning, green trees, landscape features; intimate knowledge of Hougomont's post-battle state; speaks with travelers and locals

## Themes
- **Redemptive sacrifice completed through escape**: Valjean revealed himself, saved innocent man, returned to Fantine's side, spoke final words, was arrested; then escaped toward Paris with Bishop's candlesticks and evidence of former guilt
- **Town's judgment reversed**: Perfect mayor exposed as convict; two-hour reversal of public sentiment; all good forgotten; denunciation and betrayal become gossip topics
- **Death and burial as social erasure**: Fantine subjected to promiscuousness of ashes; public grave; buried as anybody and everybody; social death parallels physical death; curé's miserliness denies her dignity
- **Maternal transcendence achieved**: Ineffable smile witnessed by Sister Simplice at moment of death indicated grace or vision beyond earthly comprehension
- **War's destruction and salvation paradox**: Hougomont chapel burned yet wooden Christ preserved with only feet blackened (miracle claim); well crammed with corpses becomes monument; nations insulted each other on chapel walls; individual deaths reduced to peasant anecdote for travelers; three thousand men fallen for sake of story
- **Providence and chance in history**: Few drops of rain decided Napoleon's downfall; cloud out of season crumbled world; Waterloo was end of Austerlitz; fate of Europe determined by minor weather variation
- **Memory and landscape**: Post-battle landscape sentient with life—buttercups, daisies, browsing horses, drying linens—yet bearing inscriptions of violence; skeletons of dead trees; blood-soaked grass; orchard bears witness to fifteen hundred men fallen in hour; garden balustrade bears bullet scratches; loopholes visible; family memories persist across generations
- **Symbolic objects and evidence**: Iron cudgel ends, stolen coin, Bishop's silver candlesticks represent Valjean's past crimes and present redemption; arranged deliberately as farewell message
